newsitem.title: GERMANY: JOBS - German unemployment, the dark before the dawn.
newsitem.headline: JOBS - German unemployment, the dark before the dawn.

text.p: In one of those utterances often heard from politicians the year before a general election, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl recently reaffirmed a government goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000.

While the swing may not come early enough either to balance Germany's books convincingly ahead of EMU or to save the current Bonn coalition, economists believe the conditions for a post-1998 upturn in the jobs market exist in abundance.

Germany's unemployment rate at 11.3 percent in January was a post-war high, and newspapers recently have predicted that February data due on Thursday will show a rise over the previous month's 4.66 million jobless.

Meanwhile though, the long-term softening of the mark, together with a Bundesbank seemingly intent on maintaining a cheap money policy for the rest of its lifetime, are already beginning to nudge the economy in the right direction.

And, a subtle shift in the behaviour of Germany's so-called "wage cartels" -- the employer federations and trade unions that dictate wage levels for entire industries -- is gradually creating a structural change in the labour market.

All of which may have been overlooked in the state of shock following January jobless figures which brought back memories of the 1930s depression, and raised the spectre of a Germany struggling to meet Maastricht criteria for 1999 entry in the single European currency.
"It can indeed be seen as a case of 'darkest before the dawn'," Alison Cottrell, economist at Paine Webber in London.
BONN REAFFIRMS GROWTH HOPES, BUSINESS MOOD BRIGHTENS

Early evidence of that came with Bonn's recent move to stand firmly by a previous forecast of 1997 economic growth at 2.5 percent, at the same time as a surprisingly strong rise in business climate perceptions from the key Ifo institute survey.

"The Ifo results in particular were the sound of German exporters giggling," said Cottrell, referring to a trade advantage she expected to be only temporarily upset by the arrival of the single European currency.
"The Euro is likely to be strong at the start because of the political will being put behind it, but after six to seven years it will still probably be soft compared to the dollar," she forecast.

She added the softness of the European currency against the dollar was likely to stem from the difficulty of a future European Central Bank in making rapid decisions influencing the course of the Euro.

The prospect of EMU has meanwhile meant the Bundesbank looks increasingly unwilling -- or unable -- to alter its monetary policy stance following the dramatic easing originally triggered by the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) crisis of 1992, some believe.
"The subjugation of the Bundesbank to EMU politics is paralysing monetary policy," Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, said.
The result, he predicted, will be that the current cheap money policy will remain in place until the replacement of the Bundesbank by the future European Central Bank.

Thus the traditional macro-economic conditions for jobs growth are already firmly in place. But according to Mayer, the really critical development is starting to take place in the jobs market itself.
"The private sector is taking over control of the labour market and the politicians are being dragged along whether they like it or not," he said.

Firms -- particularly Germany's "Mittelstand" of small and medium companies -- are increasingly abandoning the employer federations they accuse of having in the past negotiated poor wage deals for them.

Top trade union officials are meanwhile accepting that sector-wide wage agreements, often held as enforceable to the letter, should become more like guidelines on which individual workforce contracts can be based.
SIGNS OF NEW FLEXIBILITY

A case in point was the recent pact signed by workers at Siemens' Osram light-bulb unit in Augsburg, southern Germany, under which Bavarian workers have -- in a virtually unprecedented move -- agreed to work Sunday shifts.
That was enough to convince management there to promise not to consider moving production to a cheaper cost centre outside Germany.
"This is something that is happening anyway as new industries grow up where the traditional wage bargaining system has not been ingrained," said Cottrell.
Aside from the ideological debate on who the real losers and gainers are within a more flexible jobs market, economists widely hold that, if the process continues, more jobs will be created.
Political risks, both for the wider economic recovery and the evolution of the labour market, do exist.

Goldman Sach's Mayer fears that politicians under pressure to act on jobs will begin to urge a reduction of overtime work -- a move he said would take any new flexibility out of the market and ultimately lead to the export of jobs.

Cottrell noted that any failure to push through a major tax reform due for 1999, which among other things is aimed at spurring investment and economic growth by chopping corporate tax rates, could have dire repercussions for business confidence.

But while the time lag between raw employment creation and a fall in dole queues still makes Kohl's year 2000 goal look ambitious, Germany, if it makes the right decisions, might well be out of the mire on jobs by the turn of the decade.
